1.title: Claude Application Design and Configuration Management
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Claude Application Design and Configuration Management. This module covers the skills claude application design, configuration management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. How Claude interprets instructions across interfaces: Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, the A P I (application programming interface) and S D K s (software development kit). Content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene and plugin management. Configuration management: Claude dot M D, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning and plugin dependencies.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Prompt Behaves Differently
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Prompt Behaves Differently. A developer tests the claims prompt in the claude.ai chat and it works well. The same text pasted into the A P I gives a different style and misses a rule. In Claude Code a teammate gets yet another answer.

1.title: The same words, different interfaces
1.text: The same words, different interfaces. The figure shows this: Where instructions come from in each interface: you supply everything in the A P I; the apps and Claude Code add their own instructions and features.

1.title: The same words, different interfaces, continued
1.text: The same words, different interfaces, continued. A P I or client S D K s. You: the system prompt, the history, the tools. Nothing else is added. claude.ai and Desktop. Anthropic adds product instructions, features and optional project or user preferences. Claude Code. Anthropic's coding system prompt plus your Claude dot M D, rules, skills, settings and tools. Agent S D K. The agent loop and built-in tools of Claude Code as a library, configured in your code. Test in the interface you ship. A prompt tuned in a chat app is not automatically right for the A P I, because the chat app adds its own context.

1.title: The same words, different interfaces, continued
1.text: The same words, different interfaces, continued. Instructions do not travel between interfaces: project instructions in claude.ai, a system prompt in the A P I and Claude dot M D in Claude Code are separate places.

1.title: Content boundaries and schemas
1.text: Content boundaries and schemas. Separate instructions from data. Put rules in the system prompt and wrap documents and user text in clear tags, so the model knows what is data and what is an instruction (Module thirteen). Set boundaries for what the assistant should do and refuse (scope, P I I handling, no legal advice) and say how to refuse. Schema design (for tools and structured output): clear descriptions, required versus optional fields, enums for fixed sets, nullable fields when data may be missing, and a version for schemas that other systems consume.

1.title: Session hygiene
1.text: Session hygiene. One task per session. Unrelated history is noise and can mislead. Start fresh (or clear) when switching tasks. Stale context causes drift. Compact or summarize long sessions. Keeps context lean (Module nine). Do not leave secrets or private data in a shared session. Avoids leakage.

1.title: Plugin management
1.text: Plugin management. A plugin packages skills, agents, hooks and M C P (Model Context Protocol) servers as one unit installed from a marketplace; it has a manifest (.claude-plugin or plugin.json). Manage plugins deliberately: install only trusted sources, review what a plugin adds (it can run hooks and tools), enable it per project, and remember each plugin adds context cost. Exam tip: "Works in the chat app, differs in the A P I" to the interfaces supply different instructions and context; recreate the needed instructions in the A P I request.

1.title: Configuration Management
1.text: Configuration Management. The figure shows this: Layers of configuration for a Claude application: model pin, versioned prompts, Claude dot M D, settings.json, plugins and environment variables.

1.title: Configuration Management, continued
1.text: Configuration Management, continued. Claude dot M D. Persistent instructions for Claude Code: user, project (shared) and directory levels; commit the project file. settings.json. User about or dot Claude settings.json (all your projects); shared project dot Claude settings.json (commit it: team permissions, hooks, plugins, env); project local dot Claude settings.local.json (kept out of git); managed settings from the organization. Model version pinning. Use the full model I D (for example claude-sonnet-five to five) instead of an alias that moves; in Claude Code use the full name or the Anthropic default model variables. Current model I Ds are pinned snapshots.

1.title: Configuration Management, continued
1.text: Configuration Management, continued. Prompt versioning. Keep prompts in files under version control, give them a version, record changes, test with evals, roll back if quality drops. Plugin dependencies. Record plugin sources and versions, and update on purpose, because a plugin update changes behavior. Why pin: an alias or "latest" can change behavior without a code change, and your evals stop being comparable. Pin, then upgrade on purpose after running evals. Shared versus personal: put team rules in the committed project file; keep personal overrides in the local file or the user file.

1.title: Configuration Management, continued
1.text: Configuration Management, continued. Claude Code model aliases (opus, sonnet, haiku, fable, best, opusplan) follow the newest version for your provider and update over time; to pin, use the full model name or the matching environment variable. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Reproducible behavior needs a pinned model, a versioned prompt and a committed settings file; "latest" and personal settings break reproducibility. Exam tip: Prompts, schemas and settings are code: commit them, review them, test them with evals and roll them back when quality drops.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Interfaces: A P I equals only what you send; apps and Claude Code add their own instructions and features. Boundaries: Rules in system; data tagged; say how to refuse; P I I scope. Schemas: Descriptions, required or optional, enums, nullable, version. Session hygiene: One task per session, fresh start, compact, no secrets in shared sessions. Plugins: Skills plus agents plus hooks plus M C P in one unit; trusted sources; context cost; per-project. settings.json: User, shared project (commit), project local (not committed), managed. Pinning: Full model I D (pinned snapshot) or the Anthropic default model; aliases move. Prompt versioning: Files in git, version, evals, rollback.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A prompt works in the claude.ai chat but behaves differently through the A P I. What is the most likely reason? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Interfaces supply different instructions and features; the A P I contains only what you send.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team wants every developer to get the same permission rules and hooks in Claude Code. Where should they put them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The shared project settings file reaches teammates through version control.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A developer wants a personal override for one project that must not be committed. Where does it belong? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The local settings file applies to you in that project and stays out of git.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An application relies on a moving model alias instead of a full model I D, and its answers drift after the alias moves to a newer version. What is the best practice? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A pinned I D keeps behavior reproducible until you choose to upgrade.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Where should the claims prompt live so changes are reviewable and reversible? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Prompts are code: version, review, test and roll back.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which describes good session hygiene? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Focused sessions, with compaction for long ones, avoid stale and misleading context in the window.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A team installs a plugin from an unknown source because it looks useful. What is the concern? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Plugins package executable components; install trusted sources and review what they add.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A schema for claim data will be used by three other systems. What should the developer do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Systems that consume the data need a stable, documented and versioned contract so changes do not break them.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two belong in the committed project configuration of a Claude Code repository? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Shared settings and instructions are committed; keys and personal overrides are not.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: B. Question six: D. Question seven: D. Question eight: B. Question nine: D and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
